gx_front_1#1.killer: gold particles caught per 1-m sample by a 2-cm hole in placer pay gravel (bankable assay statistics)
gx_front_1#1.why: A finger-thin hole catches about one gold flake per metre even in a rich Kolyma placer, against ~20 needed for a +/-50% assay, so it cannot give bankable grade, and exploration is only ~6% of delivered cost anyway.

EC:EB:g1_loop#2.killer: share of Laptev-launched floes that reach Fram Strait
EC:EB:g1_loop#2.why: Even with chosen launch points at most half of Laptev ice ever joined the Transpolar Drift (about a fifth survives today), and bags, two years of 14% money and a token pickup already cost as much as the rail freight they replace.

EC:EB:g2_evo2#1.killer: near-bed wave orbital velocity needed to stir 0.5-mm sand in a 1-m-deep pond
EC:EB:g2_evo2#1.why: Waves on a pond this small are too short to reach the floor: even a gale stirs it at ~2 cm/s, a quarter of what 0.5-mm sand needs and ~5% of what 20-mm stones need, so the sorting that would halve placer cost never starts.

g1_mech#3.killer: yearly release volume to float 1.4 Mt of concentrate 100 km down a 20-m creek at 0.8 m depth
g1_mech#3.why: The barges fall behind the crest, so the release must run for the whole voyage, and one small-creek snowmelt carries under a quarter of a Baimskaya-size year while a free creek route would trim only the 5% outbound share.

erp2_a#3.killer: charge per kg of grain needed for the claimed 41-cm drift at 300 kV/m over a 1.5-m fall
erp2_a#3.why: Measured charging of the feldspar and quartz waste gives about half the claimed drift, and even the idea's own saving is under 3% of delivered lithium carbonate cost.

gx_fl_1#2.killer: hoop strap tension at the base of a 60-m tailings thickener holding 6 m of slurry, safety factor 4
gx_fl_1#2.why: The "a sixth of burst" check compares pressure, but strap tension grows with tank radius, so a 60-m thickener wall needs about 4x the hoop strength ever demonstrated, and the shells reach at most a quarter of capex.

g1_core2#2.killer: barrel life at ~1.5 km/s with 100-500 kg rounds
g1_core2#2.why: A gun this fast wears out its barrel in about 65 rounds against ~12,800 a day needed for Baimskaya, and the launch energy alone costs more than the whole outbound logistics bill.

gx_ledg_1#2.killer: seam area gasified per well pair
gx_ledg_1#2.why: Underground gasification itself is proven, but a well pair sweeps about 0.2 ha rather than the 1.5 ha assumed, and at 10 kt/yr the station's crew, plant and 2-3 new well pairs a year cost more than the barge and winter-road chain they remove.

EC:EB:g2_imm#3.killer: winter electricity from freezing the leach liquor vs electrowinning demand, per kg Cu (2 g/L PLS frozen 96% to reach CuSO4 saturation; Nov–Mar air −31 °C; 5 K/10 K heat-exchanger approaches; 0.6 of Carnot)
EC:EB:g2_imm#3.why: Freezing covers only ~60% of the electrowinning power (100% only if the whole season averaged −40 °C), and SX plus diesel are too small a share of cost to pay for a plant that must freeze ~480 t of liquor per tonne of copper.

EC:EB:g1_genius#3.killer: ice that must leave the sand before the dry electrostatic roll vs the "free drying" of −30 °C air
EC:EB:g1_genius#3.why: Frozen ground is not dry ground: the pore ice stays on the grains, and removing it with −30 °C air would take ~1.2×10^5 m³ of air per tonne of sand, so the gold never reaches the roll as free grains.

EC:EB:g2_evo1#3.killer: winter sublimation flux from the gravel pad
EC:EB:g2_evo1#3.why: The measured sublimation is about 1/3 of what is needed, so the pad would have to be ~3.3 km²; snowfall (~0.4 mm/day, ~5× the sublimation) buries it anyway, and the extra handling makes each ounce dearer.

g1_core2#1.killer: rate at which ponded, darkened yedoma deepens by thaw
g1_core2#1.why: A 1.5 m channel would take ~24 years to form (while the banks retreat ~1.2 m/yr), and even a finished canal only shortens one leg of the delivery chain.

EC:EB:g2_evo1#2.killer: under-ice river discharge needed to carry a season's sand (100,000 m³ of 1 mm sand over 120 days at 1.5 m/s under the keel; Meyer-Peter–Müller bedload formula)
EC:EB:g2_evo1#2.why: Placer rivers carry about 1/20 of the winter flow needed (most freeze through, or overflow as aufeis when the keel chokes them), and even a working version saves only the washing, ~8% of the chain.

g1_core2#3.killer: average amount the film surface must stay below air temperature over the thaw season to keep the thaw inside a 2 m gravel pad (Stefan formula: at most 541 °C·day of surface thawing)
g1_core2#3.why: The film supplies only ~60% of the cooling needed in the Arctic (~25% in central Yakutia), cannot be laid on driven-over or dusty surfaces, and foundations are too small a share of delivered cost for the chain to change.

gx_front_2#2.killer: ammonia made per tonne of ore ground vs ammonia the leach consumes (sulphide sulphur ends up as ammonium sulphate; ore with 1% Ni + 1% Cu)
gx_front_2#2.why: Even at the lab-record efficiency the mill makes about 1/1,000 of the ammonia the leach consumes, and if it did make it all, the electrolytic hydrogen alone ($746/t) would cost about three times the inbound logistics it removes ($255/t).

g1_mech#2.killer: reduction in hauled tonnage that dry electrostatic sorting achieves at usable recovery
g1_mech#2.why: Dry charge sorting achieves about half the required tonnage cut at worse recovery than the dense-media and flotation plants already concentrating on site, so the hauled tonnage does not fall and delivered cost rises.

gx_front_1#3.killer: specific energy to loosen frozen ground
gx_front_1#3.why: Even for the weakest stone type and only the ice volume, burst-wave fatigue needs 13x the energy the whole dozer fleet now spends per m3, so battery rigs would cost about $5,200/oz in power alone.

g1_loop#2.killer: fraction of pods (Siberian-shelf ice) that reach Fram Strait
g1_loop#2.why: At most about 20% of shelf ice now survives to Fram Strait, but the pods need about 89% to break even, so each delivered tonne costs about $800 against $130 by sea.

gx_fl_1#4.killer: site electricity per t LCE (salt splitting plus flash heating)
gx_fl_1#4.why: The scheme swaps reagents for 3.6x the electricity today's energy budget buys at winter-road diesel power, so it would survive only on a grid at about 11 rub/kWh or less, which a winter-road site does not have.

gx_ledg_1#3.killer: lithium the alumina hydrate can carry within smelter spec
gx_ledg_1#3.why: Lithium co-precipitates with the hydrate as intended, but 45 kt/yr would then need a full-stream strip removing 97.6% of it from all of Achinsk's alumina hydrate, not a small new circuit (and RUSAL said in Aug 2026 it may close Pikalyovo).

gx_front_2#3.why: Even the weakest kidney stones need 6x the energy of a whole crushing plant per tonne, and at realistic kimberlite strengths the cost rises to about $75/ct.

gx_front_2#1.killer: surplus power needed to heat the full ore stream to 600 C
gx_front_2#1.why: Heating every tonne needs 3.3x the site's entire generation, and the 19% easier grinding (Minerals 2022 12(5):593) returns only 2% of the charge energy, so each kWh pays about 1.02 times, not twice.

gx_fl_1#3.killer: settlements with a coal deposit within about 100 km on their river
gx_fl_1#3.why: The economics are strong because the 85% logistics share collapses, but the idea works only where coal outcrops on the same river, at most about 40% of Arctic Yakutia's settlements, so it needs a field inventory of coal bluffs and water-protection-zone permits.

g1_genius#3.killer: gold recovery with dry separation of frozen gravel
g1_genius#3.why: Measured dry recovery falls short of break-even, and even at equal recovery year-round dry work saves only about 17%, because earthmoving and mineral extraction tax dominate the cost.

gx_front_2#4.killer: fraction of gold left in the calcine after a ~3,000 °C flash (Au boils at 2,856 °C; p_Au ≈ 1.7 atm; a 1-µm grain evaporates in ~17 µs)
gx_front_2#4.why: At 3,000 °C the gold boils off with the arsenic. Even if it stayed, the container only replaces a ~$250/oz link (POX capex $46/oz, POX opex ≤$122/oz, freight $81/oz), while its 939 kWh/t of flash power at 41 rub/kWh costs ~$223/oz (RATIO 1.09 even at NPP power prices).

gx_fl_2#5.killer: pump pressure per 15-km hose segment at the −57.8 °C record low (ESPO-type crude at 6.95 cSt @20 °C, extrapolated with the Siberian Light slope to 124 cSt; laminar flow; +100 m rise)
gx_fl_2#5.why: The strapped hose survives the hydraulics, but trucking is only $10 of an $82/bbl chain that is ~53% tax. The hose alone ($180/m aramid-TPU catalogue price, shop.midwesthose.com, $54M) amortises to $6.5/bbl, and even the claimed $1/bbl reaches only 1.12.

gx_ledg_2#2.killer: diesel per gram to hot-water thaw, jet and airlift the paystreak (20 vol% pore ice = 69 MJ/m³; 60% of heat reaches the ore; 85% boiler; grade 1.75 g/m³; 85% recovery)
gx_ledg_2#2.why: Ideal thaw alone already takes 1.5 l/g, so the 2 l/g claim fails. Each cased 0.3-m hole through 20 m of cover yields only ~2.7 oz and costs ≥$3,900 even at US double-cased rates (softlive.floridadep.gov). That adds ~$1,440/oz, more than the stripping fleet it removes.

gx_fl_2#4.killer: flash Joule heating (FJH) throughput for run-of-mine pegmatite (1.96 Mt/yr; 43.6 t ore per t LCE; 210 MW, or 140 MW after the thermophotovoltaic recapture)
gx_fl_2#4.why: The chemistry works in the lab, but the pit needs ~1,000x the largest FJH plant that exists. Heating all 43.6 t of ore per tonne also costs 27 MWh/t ($2,094/t at 6.45 rub/kWh), so even the claimed tenfold process-capex cut gives only ~1.2x.

gx_fl_2#1.killer: diesel to thaw the scoring slots (0.2-m back, side and base slots on 10×3×8.3 m slabs = 11% of volume; 30 vol% ice; 100% heat use) against one-tenth of today's dozer diesel
gx_fl_2#1.why: The <1 bar cushions can tip a slab (6x the restoring moment). But melting even the thinnest slots takes about as much diesel per m³ as ripping and dozing does now, ~7x the claimed one-tenth budget.

gx_ledg_2#5.killer: dredging depth to the pit floor (70 Mt/yr ore × ~25 yr × strip ratio 0.8 = 1.17 km³ → 230–390 m mean depth over 3–5 km²; ~47 m of deepening in year 1 on 1 km²; ore traced to 750 m)
gx_ledg_2#5.why: No dredge reaches below ~45 m, so the floating mine stalls within the first year or two of a pit that must go several hundred metres deep. Even the claimed capital halving, with no dredge or barge cost added, gives only 1.26x.

EC:EB:g1_core2#1.killer: water needed to hold barge depth in the gravity-graded channel after the lake drains (1.5 m × 15 m for ≤400-t Kolyma barges; n 0.03; slope 0.1 m/km → 8.7 m³/s over a 100-day season)
EC:EB:g1_core2#1.why: Lake heat could cut the gully: about 86,000 m³ of 12 °C water per km melts the 65–90 vol% yedoma ice (epic.awi.de/35773). But water draining to the river leaves no navigable canal behind, and the road leg it replaces is a few percent of delivered cost.

gx_ledg_1#5.killer: throughput per rope-conveyor line at 25 Mt/yr and 85% availability
gx_ledg_1#5.why: The comparison is with Elga's own railway at ~$12/t (built for ~100 bn rub, about $2.2M/km), not the $46/t RZD tariff. A 450-km elevated belt costs more per tonne: $3.2bn → $16.8/t (from bulk-online's $2.07M/km at 10 Mtpa, scaled), or $45/t at Thundersaid's average $0.1/t-km. It would also need ~3x the capacity and ~90x the length of any RopeCon built.

EC:EB:g1_loop#1.killer: spare laden-leg deadweight of the Arctic LNG fleet vs whole-ore tonnage
EC:EB:g1_loop#1.why: A laden Arc7 has only ~6,200 t of deadweight to spare, so the whole fleet could carry about 2% of one Baimskaya's ore, and river-barging 233 t of ore per tonne of copper alone costs about as much as today's entire delivered chain.

gx_front_1#2.killer: post-flood summer discharge needed to hold a 1.0 m x 12 m barge lane (Manning, n 0.035, slope 0.0005)
gx_front_1#2.why: Wing dams can narrow a channel but cannot add water: small Yakutian rivers carry about a third of the post-flood flow a minimal barge lane needs, and the large chain gain holds only if the robot works cost almost nothing.

gx_front_2#5.killer: survey line density over the territory
gx_front_2#5.why: Fixed logistics corridors give about 1/400 of the line density a kimberlite search needs, and exploration is only ~2% of delivered gold cost, so even a perfect free survey barely moves the chain.

gx_ledg_2#3.why: Borehole-mining physics has headroom, but at ~200 t per hole a village boiler needs ~23 new permafrost wells a year plus a full-time crew and plant, which leaves only ~1.2x over imported coal (and less where a shallow seam could simply be pit-mined).

EC:EB:g1_core#1.killer: water-limited washing throughput of the staircase (Meyer-Peter-Muller bedload at 1% slope, 30 mm gravel, 1.5 m2/s lane flow = 215 m3 water per m3 ore, water reused at 5 weirs)
EC:EB:g1_core#1.why: The water roughly suffices, but the staircase replaces only the washing plant, not the stripping of frozen overburden that is two-thirds of physical placer cost, so its best case is ~15% cheaper even before recovery losses from washing unscreened ore.

g1_core#1.killer: seasonal tonnage the pulses can lift over the shoals (Manning: 47 m3/s for 1.2 m depth over a 40 m shoal, ~4,000 s per pulse, 4 x 500 t barges, 100 open-water days, est.)
g1_core#1.why: Even with the pulses moving two-thirds of the needed tonnage, the road and trucking they replace are under 10% of delivered copper cost, so the chain gain stays below 1.1.

gx_ledg_1#1.why: The trench the highwall miner needs and the pillars it leaves cap the earthmoving cut near 2.8x rather than 8-10x (8x is unreachable unless overburden exceeds ~6x the pay thickness), which still leaves a real but modest ~1.25x.

g1_loop#1.killer: spare laden-leg deadweight of the Arc7 fleet vs concentrate tonnage
g1_loop#1.why: The whole Arc7 fleet's spare deadweight could at best carry one Baimskaya's concentrate, but sea freight is only 5% of delivered copper cost, so free carriage cannot beat ~1.05x.

gx_fl_2#3.killer: peak vertical gravity gradient of a one-winter coal lens (3,000 t, 27x27x3 m, top 4.5 m, coal 1.35 vs host 2.3 t/m3, prism model) vs 3-sigma detection
gx_fl_2#3.why: The haul saving is real (2.2x) but even with stationary 20 E noise the gradiometer only just sees a one-winter lens, so lens-finding by sled tow is unproven and ground-ice bodies, lighter than coal, will give false targets.

EC:EB:g1_core#2.killer: flush water through the bowl vs water needed to carry its copper out in a 25-yr life (30 m x 2.7 t/m3 x 0.4% Cu x 60% recovery = 194 kg Cu/m2, PLS 3 g/L)
EC:EB:g1_core#2.why: Snow and rain bring about a quarter of the solution needed (0.71 even at an 8 g/L PLS), so a 30-m bowl would take about 94 years and still give up the gold credit that makes the current route cheap.

gx_ledg_1#4.killer: water depth on the tow route vs draft of a 10 Mt/yr module (1,240 t/h; ~18 kt of mills, mill charge, flotation slurry and heated superstructure -> ~28 kt displacement -> 4.7-6.3 m draft; Akademik Lomonosov, 21.5 kt on 144x30 m at 5.6 m draft, as real-world check)
gx_ledg_1#4.why: The module draws more than twice the depth Siberian rivers guarantee, and with pit, tailings, road, port and power still onshore, even a 6.5x cheaper concentrator cuts delivered cost only about 13%.

g1_mech#1.killer: packet drift speed under ice vs the claimed 25 km/day (1-t sack ~1 m3, 1% net buoyancy pressing on the ice, sliding friction 0.01-0.03, drag coefficient 1, flow next to the ice 0.8 of mean)
g1_mech#1.why: Measured winter currents under Siberian river ice are about half the speed needed, and friction against the ice cuts packet speed to about 4-7 km/day, a 4-7x shortfall before pressure ridges and hanging ice dams are counted.

EC:EB:g1_core2#3.killer: net cooling flux of a tray held just past the eutectic (-52 C, air -45 C) vs the heat to freeze a 1-cm brine layer in a 16-h night (eutectic ice + CaCl2.6H2O ~180 kJ/kg, 1,280 kg/m3)
EC:EB:g1_core2#3.why: At -50 C even a perfect window emitter radiates only ~28 W/m2, so the trays cannot sit 10 K below air while also giving up freezing heat, and the tray area pushes concentrate cost to about ten times the price of finished carbonate.

g1_genius#2.killer: river-ice capacity for the lightest mainline diesel, 2TE116 at 2 x 138 t (Gold P = A h^2, safe A = 3.5 kg/cm2)
g1_genius#2.why: Thickened late-winter ice carries only about half a two-section locomotive and far less in early winter, and track capital is so small a slice of delivered coal cost that the cheaper line saves under 5%.

gx_front_1#4.killer: ore throughput one open-gradient superconducting coil can treat vs one pit's ore stream (4 Mt/yr over 7,000 h, Lomonosov GOK 1 + 3 Mt/yr modules, Rapaport/IDEX)
gx_front_1#4.why: One coil treats only about a sixth of a mid-size pit's ore even at the best theoretical rate, and because mining dominates kimberlite cost, a perfect 3x plant shrink would cut delivered cost only about 12%.

gx_front_1#5.killer: 20-year thaw settlement under a heated building on grade vs cell stroke (1-D Stefan model: +20 C inside, floor R 5.2 m2K/W, thawed-soil conductivity 1.4 W/mK, 40 vol% ice, latent heat 334 kJ/kg -> 10.7 m thaw, thaw strain 0.2)
gx_front_1#5.why: With no air gap, a heated building thaws raw ice-rich ground 7-11 m deep in 20 years and settles 1.5-2 m, more than the cells can make up, and foundations are too small a share of delivered cost to matter.

EC:EB:g2_evo1#1.killer: depth-mean under-ice current needed for a +1% buoyant 1 m³ pod to slide along the channel ceiling (friction 0.05, near-ice factor 0.69) and cover 500 km in a 120-day window
EC:EB:g2_evo1#1.why: Even if the berm channel forms and the pods creep along it, buoyant pods cost about as much per tonne as the summer ore barge they replace, so delivered cost barely moves (ratio 0.96-1.11 across haul length and pod reuse).

erp2_b#4.killer: mean under-ice velocity to roll the 1.6 m, +750 kg log over 5-20 cm ice keels
erp2_b#4.why: Measured winter currents are about a quarter of what is needed to roll the logs over ordinary 5 cm keels (0.40 even in the fastest delta channel), so the attractive coal ratio is never reached.

g1_loop#3.killer: depth-mean current for a +1% buoyant torpedo pod (Cd 0.2) to slide on even a perfectly smooth ice underside and reach a port 1,000 km away within a 120-day window
g1_loop#3.why: The torpedo shape minimises the drag that has to push it, so the pod needs about 4x the measured winter current, and even free pods would only trim a river leg worth about 5% of delivered copper cost (maximum ratio 1.06).

g1_core#3.killer: annual heat balance of the 70 °C storage layer at Yakutsk with a 1.18 m gradient zone and zero heat extraction
g1_core#3.why: At 62°N a standard gradient pond cannot even hold 70 °C with zero output (only a 4.4 m gradient breaks even), its best power at the idea's 60-80 °C costs about 2.5x diesel, and even free power would cap the ratio at 1.11.

gx_fl_1#5.killer: largest feed particle the steel-needle field mill can break
gx_fl_1#5.why: A 1x10 mm needle carries about 3 mJ against roughly 5 J to break a 16 mm particle, so the pipe cannot take the mills' duty, and grinding capex is too small a share for a 10x cut to pass 1.1 (1.13 only if grinding were free).

EC:EB:g1_mech#3.killer: water-to-gravel ratio the heat coupling delivers to the riffled chute (101 MJ/m³ ice-cemented gravel, 10 °C sun-warmed water)
EC:EB:g1_mech#3.why: Washing is only about 8% of delivered placer-gold cost, so even free washing gives only 1.09, and the heat-coupled slurry is too thick for a riffled chute (margin 0.29 at 15 °C).

erp2_b#2.killer: water-to-gravel ratio at the design point (loose pile 50-55 MJ/m³, 5-7 °C water)
erp2_b#2.why: Face-thaw headroom is ample (88x), but the design slurry has about half the water real sluices use, and a 2.3x cut to an 8% link moves delivered cost by only about 5%.

EC:EB:g1_core2#2.killer: gun barrel life against the shot rate for 1.4 Mt/yr of concentrate at 0.5 t payload per shot
EC:EB:g1_core2#2.why: A gun throwing 0.5 t at 0.7-0.8 km/s wears out a barrel about every hour at Baimskaya scale (about every 30 h even for a 50 kt/yr mine), and even a wear-free diesel-fired launcher reaches only 1.02.

erp2_a#1.killer: CO needed to keep 0.027 mol% Ni(CO)4 stable at the 45 °C compressor-discharge cap, 9.8 MPa
erp2_a#1.why: The chemistry works with 1.5x headroom, but the pipeline adds about $930/t Ni to save $27/t of rail freight, so the whole chain costs about 9 % more than refining and railing or selling concentrate.

gx_ledg_2#1.killer: push force to slide an 8,000-t block over its thawed paystreak vs shear reaction of the next frozen block's base
gx_ledg_2#1.why: The block can be pushed with about 1.5x reaction headroom and the kerfs cost only 0.13 l/m³, but drilling and jacking make overburden about 2.9x cheaper rather than 10x, so delivered cost falls about 28 %, short of the 1.5x bar.

EC:EB:g2_imm#1.killer: nickel supply from a deposit on the Power of Siberia route to fill 0.1 mol% Ni(CO)4 in 38 bcm/yr (92.7 kt Ni/yr)
EC:EB:g2_imm#1.why: No deposit on the route can feed 100 kt/yr (the largest supplies a third of that), and the pipeline swaps about $70/t of freight for about $610/t of CO and decomposition, so the chain gets dearer.

EC:EB:g1_loop#3.killer: river drag on a pod pressed against the ice underside vs ice-on-ice friction from its own buoyancy
EC:EB:g1_loop#3.why: Buoyant pods need about 3x more force than a 0.29 m/s winter current supplies to slide along the ice, pods frozen at −40 °C carry about 63 MJ of cold that freezes about 190 kg of water onto them on contact, and hauling whole ore barely beats concentrating on site (1.10x even at 5 % Cu).

EC:EB:g2_imm#2.killer: heap-leach rate at −30 °C as a fraction of the +15 °C summer rate
EC:EB:g2_imm#2.why: At −30 °C the leach runs at about a sixth of summer speed, so year-round leaching raises annual heap output only about 1.24x, and the salt lost with spent ore costs more than the carbon, elution and gold-room steps that the crude ride removes.

g1_core#2.killer: thaw depth after 3 seasons in a 1-D enthalpy model (Susuman: mean annual air −11.5 °C, July +15 °C; black film n_t 2.0, top of the asphalt range 1.4–2.3; deep snow n_f 0.25; 30 % ice; natural active layer 1.55 m, permafrost −5.8 °C)
g1_core#2.why: The film and fences add only about 1 m to the first summer's thaw and then advance about 0.1 m a year, so most of the cut stays frozen and delivered cost falls by about 4 %.

EC:EB:g1_genius#1.killer: share of pods placed on young ice off the Laptev fast ice that reach Fram Strait in the Transpolar Drift
EC:EB:g1_genius#1.why: Most pods would be released on the shelf when their ice melts rather than ride to Fram Strait, and single-use tagged pods carrying run-of-mine ore cost several times the value of the copper they deliver.

EC:EB:g1_mech#1.killer: share of fixed-bladder 1-t packages whose net lift falls in the 0–34 kg window where they both float and are dragged along the ice (drag 50 N at 0.29 m/s vs μ 0.15)
EC:EB:g1_mech#1.why: Even with shells warmed to 0 °C, about a third of fixed-bladder packages either sink or stick under the ice, and moving 23 t of ordinary ore per ounce costs more than the plant and power it saves.

gx_ledg_2#4.killer: cold-crude throughput of a 300-km 12" lay-flat TPU hose at its rated pressure (crude cools to the ~-30 °C snow bed with a ~22 km e-fold length; ~36 cSt, laminar Re~2,100)
gx_ledg_2#4.why: Hydraulically workable only if the crude really pours at -40 °C (an ESPO-blend -20 °C pour point would gel in the snow bed), but trucking is only 12% of a tax-dominated cost, so even a free hose caps the gain at 1.14x, and the seasonal peak-capacity capex wipes out the rest.

EC:EB:g1_core#3.killer: winter (Nov-Apr, ice-covered) heat balance of the 70 °C bottom brine at Udokan latitude 57°N
EC:EB:g1_core#3.why: With nothing drawn off, the brine still falls to ~42 °C by end-February, so the year-round 60-80 °C leach-and-power claim fails, and even on the annual balance 270 m2 of lined, salted, insulated pond per annual tonne costs about as much as the concentrator and fuel it replaces.

g1_genius#1.killer: fraction of Laptev-shelf ice, with the containers in it, that survives into the Transpolar Drift and reaches Fram Strait
g1_genius#1.why: Four of every five containers melt out before the drift, and the box alone costs about six times the ore's value per delivered tonne.

EC:EB:g2_evo2#2.killer: drag needed to push the lead 1-m sphere (0.5% positively buoyant, net lift 25.7 N) down and under a 29° ice-keel face
EC:EB:g2_evo2#2.why: Ropes cannot push, so the lead sphere stalls at the first keel and bonds into the growing ice (adfreeze 0.1-1.6 MPa, trid.trb.org 296123) within ~2-3 h, and even free logistics could cut this chain by only 8% (ceiling 1.09).

EC:EB:g1_genius#2.killer: river-ice bearing capacity at crossings for a 138-t six-axle locomotive section (Gold's formula P = A h², A = 3.5 kg/cm²)
EC:EB:g1_genius#2.why: Flooding or spray ice (up to 50-80 cm/day, e3s-conferences emmft2023_08015) can push crossings past 2 m only from mid-winter, shortening the 5-6-month season, and the ~1.3-1.5x saving comes mainly from moving the plant off permafrost, not from cheap haulage.

EC:EB:g1_mech#2.killer: finest particle size that free-fall electrostatic stages can separate vs the liberation (regrind) size needed for shipping-grade Cu concentrate
EC:EB:g1_mech#2.why: Shipping-grade liberation needs particles about 2.5x finer than free-fall electrostatics can sort, and because remote mines already ship flotation concentrate, the cascade can only trim part of a 15% processing share.

gx_fl_1#1.killer: thickness of frozen ground an excavator can dig without pre-loosening (blasting, ripping or thawing)
gx_fl_1#1.why: An excavator bucket cannot advance into a fully frozen gravel face (underground permafrost placer mines blast it), and even if it could, a 5-6x higher cost per m3 underground eats most of the 5-10x volume cut.

gx_fl_2#2.killer: frozen pay gravel cut and delivered per robot-shift needed for tenfold-less-ground underground mining to beat open-cut earthmoving per gram
gx_fl_2#2.why: Cutting bedrock drifts in winter is physically workable and could save about a quarter, because taxes and washing stay, but the black-sand steering is unproven (gold concentrates far more strongly than magnetite in the same gravels, archives.datapages.com Day & Fletcher 1991) and the gain shrinks to ~1.1x if robots cost $2M.

gx_res1_b#5.killer: loaded draft of a 5,000-8,000 t barge vs guaranteed depth on settlement rivers
gx_res1_b#5.why: Using the barge's idle winter as the boilerhouse does cut delivered cost about 1.6x, but a 5,000-8,000 t hull draws ~3.75 m against <=2 m guaranteed depth (none at all on most of the network), so it reaches only main-stem settlements, which are already the cheapest to supply, not "nearly every river settlement".

gx_res1_b#4.killer: gold exposed per km of eroding pay-bearing bank per year (retreat x pay thickness x grade)
gx_res1_b#4.why: Pay-bearing banks are gravel-floored, retreat <=1 m/yr and big-river alluvium carries <=0.3 g/m3, so the river exposes only ~0.45 kg of gold per km per year, and even 50 km of auriferous bank gives ~22 kg/yr at a cost above open cut.

gx_res1_b#10.killer: brine inflow that fills the pit lake (the lake's lithium supply)
gx_res1_b#10.why: The brine is rich enough, but it enters at only ~300 m3/h, which caps output near 2 kt LCE/yr where DLE costs over twice today's spodumene route, and flooding pits above live or planned underground mines is exactly how Mir flooded in 2017.

gx_res1_b#7.killer: field-dried yield per ha on undrained permafrost peat
gx_res1_b#7.why: Drying looks physically feasible in dry central-Yakutian summers even with a ~2.5x penalty for undrainable permafrost peat, but a small, Far-North-built robotic peat chain delivers heat only ~1.4x cheaper than barged coal, short of removing most of the 85% logistics share, with high-ash peat and frozen stacks as further risks.

gx_res1_b#3.killer: survival of pillars and openings 35-75 years after abandonment (pillar stress vs long-term strength of frozen gravel)
gx_res1_b#3.why: If the pillars still stood, 3-10 g/m3 would make robotic recovery about 2x cheaper than open cut, but pillars sized for months carried ~3 MPa against ~1.25 MPa long-term strength, so after decades most will have crept, crushed and caved, closing the "already paid" access.

gx_res1_b#9.why: Mining excavators fail every ~80-100 h while a crewless season needs ~2,000 h unattended (plus 110-1,100 m3 of diesel per placer at 11 l/g), and even a flawless robot set removes only ~24% of cost (ceiling ratio 1.32).

gx_res1_b#1.killer: excavation-and-lift rate of one borehole tool in frozen placer gravel
gx_res1_b#1.why: The hole is small enough (hole volume is 0.03 of the pay volume), but at the only measured borehole rate in frozen gravel a bell costs more per m³ of pay than open-cut stripping, and drilling plus moving the tool already cost ~$16/g, against the ~$1.6/g of earthmoving that halving delivered cost would allow.

gx_res1_b#8.killer: cutting radius of a rotating water jet in coal from a borehole
gx_res1_b#8.why: At the measured jet reach a 150 m hole yields about 97 t instead of 5,000 t, so drilling rises from 0.03 to ~1.5 m per tonne and coal at the boiler would cost about 40,000 rub/t against 23,000 now.

gx_res1_b#12.killer: residual gold grade in old dredge-pond tailings against break-even
gx_res1_b#12.why: The grade is about twice break-even, but with diesel power, ~65% recovery of fine gold and MET unchanged the whole chain is only about 1.4x cheaper (1.3-1.5x for 55-75% recovery), and Kolyma dumps already reworked three to five times (www1.ru, 2 Sep 2026) may hold less.

gx_res1_b#2.killer: share of the placer's gold inside a 0.4 m basal slot
gx_res1_b#2.why: Most of the gold probably lies outside a 0.4 m slot, and even at the claimed share the cost of cutting by robot keeps the whole-chain gain near 1.4x (about 1.1x at the measured share).

gx_res1_b#6.killer: water depth at a coal-seam face where a 50,000 t ship must moor
gx_res1_b#6.why: No Bering-field seam meets water deep enough for the ship: the mined seam is far inland and even the port's coast is barge-depth, and against an operator's own short haul road and port the saving would only be ~1.25x anyway.

gx_res1_b#11.killer: depth of the thawed zone under a thermokarst lake deeper than 2 m, against depth to pay
gx_res1_b#11.why: The thaw runs well below the pay and dredging pre-thawed gravel cuts the chain about 1.6x even with new-dredge capital and winter heating, but the measured lake is in an Arctic coastal lowland, not a placer valley, so the open risk is how many deep lakes actually sit on placers; the reservoir variant fails, since ~40 years of thaw is only ~14 m and the Kolyma reservoir's ~33 m mean depth leaves just ~12 m of the 45 m reach.
